title: American Music
description: Ten short stories, letters, diaries and reports about American music: jazz in New Orleans, the blues, a banjo diary, a gospel choir, Nashville, a lake festival, how ears hear notes, an old music hall, the story of rock and roll and a visit to Memphis.

lessons.title: A Jazz Evening in New Orleans
lessons.summary: In an e-mail, Anna tells her friend about the Sixth Ward, a rainy evening in a jazz club and an old drummer who plays with brushes.
lessons.text:
Subject: Hello from New Orleans

Hi Ben,

I have been in New Orleans for 3 days now, and I already have so many impressions that I hardly know where to start. My first impression was the heat. Even though it is only May, the air is hot and wet, so in the afternoon I usually sit on a bench in the shade of a big old tree and drink something cold.

Yesterday I took a walking tour of the Tremé, which is one of the oldest Black neighborhoods in the country. Many people here also call it the Sixth Ward. Our guide explained that the city is divided into 17 wards, and that people often use the ward numbers when they talk about where they live. Jazz grew up in neighborhoods like this one more than 100 years ago. In the Tremé there is a square where, before the Civil War, enslaved Africans used to meet on Sunday afternoons to play music and dance. The guide said this was one reason why the music of New Orleans is so unusual.

In the evening, it started to pour. The rain poured down for an hour, so I ran into a small club and found a seat on a bench near the stage. A band of 5 players was on stage. The man on the drums was an older gentleman in a white hat. Instead of sticks, he was playing with brushes. A brush is a short handle with many thin wires at one end, and it gives a much softer sound than a stick. The gentleman played so softly that I could hear the rain on the roof alongside the music.

What I found unusual was that nobody had any music on paper. The players simply played alongside each other and listened carefully. After the show, I asked the gentleman how long he had been playing. He told me that he had been playing in that club for 40 years and that his father had played there before him. He also said the brushes in his hand were older than me!

Tomorrow I'm going to take a boat trip on the Mississippi. The boat sails twice a day, and a jazz band plays on it while it sails up and down the river. I'll tell you all about it when I get home.

Your friend,
Anna

Questions:
Where does Anna sit in the afternoon, and why?
She sits on a bench in the shade of a big old tree because the air is hot and wet.
What do many people call the Tremé?
Many people call it the Sixth Ward.
Why did Anna go into the club?
She went into the club because it started to pour.
What is a brush?
A brush is a short handle with many thin wires at one end.
What did the older gentleman tell Anna?
He told her that he had been playing in that club for 40 years and that his father had played there before him.
How often does the boat sail?
It sails twice a day.

lessons.title: Where the Blues Came From
lessons.summary: A short report on how the blues began among poor farm workers in the Mississippi Delta and how it spread.
lessons.text:
The blues is one of the most important kinds of American music. It began in the South around 1900, especially in the Mississippi Delta, a flat area of rich farm land in the state of Mississippi.

Most of the people who first played the blues were African Americans who lived in deep poverty. Many of them worked on land that belonged to someone else. They grew crops such as cotton, and at the end of the year they had to give a large part of the crop to the owner of the land. A family could pick tons of cotton in a year and still have almost no money. In spite of this poverty, people found ways to make music. They sang in the fields and played cheap guitars in the evening.

A blues song usually tells a simple narrative. A man loses his job, a woman leaves her home, or a farmer watches his crop fail. The narrative is almost always told in the first person.

The blues also has some clear characteristics. One characteristic is its form: many blues songs are built on 12 bars, and each verse has three lines. The first line is sung twice, and the third line answers it. Another characteristic is the "blue note", a note that is sung or played a little lower than people expect. The blue note gives the music its sad, special sound.

Between 1910 and 1970, millions of Black Southerners left the South for work elsewhere, especially in northern cities such as Chicago and Detroit. They took their music with them. In Chicago, players such as Muddy Waters began to play the blues on electric guitars, because the city clubs were loud and crowded. This was an important step in the evolution of the blues. The evolution continued, and the blues helped to create rhythm and blues and, later, rock and roll.

In the years after 1960, young British bands such as the Rolling Stones played the blues and spoke about the old blues singers who had influenced them. Thanks to them, awareness of the blues grew in America as well. As awareness grew, some older blues singers were invited to play for new, young audiences, both in America and elsewhere.

Questions:
Where did the blues begin?
It began in the South, especially in the Mississippi Delta.
Why did many families have almost no money?
Even if a family picked tons of cotton, it had to give a large part of the crop to the owner of the land.
What kind of narrative does a blues song usually tell?
It usually tells a simple narrative about a hard life, and it is told in the first person.
What are two characteristics of the blues?
One characteristic is its form of 12 bars and three lines per verse, and another is the blue note.
Why did players in Chicago use electric guitars?
They used electric guitars because the city clubs were loud and crowded.
How did British bands help the blues in America?
They raised awareness of the blues, so some older singers were invited to play for young audiences.

lessons.title: My Banjo Diary
lessons.summary: Over five weeks, a beginner learns to play the banjo with the help of a teacher, a sister and a kind neighbor.
lessons.text:
Monday, March 3

Today I finally bought a banjo! I have wanted one since I heard a bluegrass band at a friend's party last summer. My first lesson with my teacher, Mr. Hill, is on Saturday.

Saturday, March 8

Mr. Hill showed me how to hold the banjo and told me a little of its history. He said that the first banjos in America were made by enslaved Africans, who built them from simple materials, based on instruments they remembered from West Africa. Then he wrote a practice plan for me with three bullet points. The first bullet point says, "Practice for 20 minutes every day." The second says, "Play slowly and carefully." The third bullet point says, "Do the finger drill 10 times." The drill is a simple exercise: my right hand plays the strings in the same order again and again, using my thumb and two fingers. "Don't worry if it sounds awful at first," Mr. Hill said. "Everybody sounds awful at first."

Tuesday, March 11

He was right. I did the drill for 20 minutes, and the sound was horrible. It was the ugliest sound I have ever made. I was afraid that my neighbor, Mrs. Green, who lives on the other side of the wall, could hear it. In the evening I knocked on her door to apologize. I apologized for the noise, but she just smiled. She said that she used to play the piano and that I didn't need to apologize. She said she liked hearing someone learn.

Thursday, March 20

A hard day. My fingers hurt, and the drill still sounded horrible, so I told my sister that I would sell the banjo. She tried to convince me to keep going. It took her ten minutes to convince me, but in the end I practiced for another 20 minutes, slowly and carefully.

Saturday, March 29

Mr. Hill said my drill sounded much better. He has adapted a simple old song for me. He took out the difficult parts, so now it is short and easy. "When you get better, we will adapt it again and add the hard parts back," he said.

Saturday, April 5

Today I played the song successfully from beginning to end! It didn't sound ugly at all. Mr. Hill said I had played it successfully on my first try. Later, my neighbor told me that she had heard it through the wall and that it sounded lovely.

Questions:
What are the three bullet points in the practice plan?
Practice for 20 minutes every day, play slowly and carefully, and do the finger drill 10 times.
What did Mr. Hill say about the sound at first?
He said that everybody sounds awful at first.
Why did the writer go to Mrs. Green's door?
The writer went to apologize for the noise.
Who tried to convince the writer to keep going?
The writer's sister tried to convince the writer to keep going.
How did Mr. Hill adapt the song?
He took out the difficult parts, so it became short and easy.
What happened on April 5?
The writer played the song successfully from beginning to end.

lessons.title: A New Voice in the Choir
lessons.summary: Grace, a teenager who came to Atlanta as a refugee, joins a gospel choir and sings in her first big concert.
lessons.text:
Grace was 16 when she came to Atlanta with her mother and her little brother. They were refugees from South Sudan. Life in a new country was not easy, and Grace missed many things from home. Most of all, she missed singing with the other girls at her old church.

One Sunday, Grace and her mother went to a church near their apartment. The gospel choir there had 40 singers. When they started to sing, Grace felt happiness for the first time in months. After the service, she went to speak to the director of the choir, Mrs. Ruth Carter.

"Can a refugee join the choir?" Grace asked in a low voice.

Mrs. Carter smiled. "Whoever loves to sing is welcome here," she said.

The choir was getting ready for its big spring concert, and the preparation took a lot of time. The singers met twice a week, on Wednesday evenings and on Saturday mornings. During the preparation, Mrs. Carter taught them to breathe well and to listen to each other. Grace learned the songs quickly, even though some of the English words were new to her.

The concert was going to be a formal event. The singers would wear long blue robes, and the guests would wear formal clothes. Grace had never sung at such a formal concert before, and she was nervous.

On the evening of the concert, the church was full. When Mrs. Carter raised her hands, the room became silent. For a few seconds, everyone was silent, and Grace could hear her own heart. Then Mrs. Carter leaned toward her and said softly, "Just sing the way you sing at home." Grace leaned forward a little, closed her eyes and began to sing.

In the middle of the concert, Grace sang a short part alone. Her voice was clear and strong. When the last song ended, the guests stood up and cheered for a long time. The singers bowed, and then they bowed once more.

After the concert, Grace's mother embraced her for a long time. Many of the singers embraced her too. "It was a privilege to sing with all of you," Grace told them. Mrs. Carter answered that it was a privilege for the choir to have such a voice. Walking home that night, Grace felt pure happiness. She had found a second home.

Questions:
Why did Grace come to Atlanta?
She came with her mother and her little brother as a refugee from South Sudan.
What did Mrs. Carter say when Grace asked to join?
She said that whoever loves to sing is welcome.
How often did the choir meet during the preparation?
The singers met twice a week, on Wednesday evenings and Saturday mornings.
Why was Grace nervous?
She was nervous because she had never sung at such a formal concert before.
What did Mrs. Carter say to Grace before the first song?
She said, "Just sing the way you sing at home."
What did Grace say after the concert?
She said that it was a privilege to sing with all of them.

lessons.title: A Weekend in Nashville
lessons.summary: A girl and her father visit Nashville, see an exhibition at the country music museum and the old Ryman Auditorium, and go to the Grand Ole Opry.
lessons.text:
Last month, my dad and I spent a weekend in Nashville, Tennessee, which people often call "Music City." Dad grew up on a small farm with 20 cows, and he loves country music. When he was a boy, his grandfather used to listen to the Grand Ole Opry on the radio every Saturday night after he had milked the cows. The Opry started as a radio show in 1925.

On Saturday morning, we went to the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum. I wasn't a big fan of country music, but I was curious. The museum had a special exhibition about the stage clothes of country singers. It included dozens of jackets covered in bright colors and shiny stones. One white jacket had small black and white cows on the arms! I was curious about who had worn it. The card said it belonged to a singer who had also grown up on a farm.

There was also a photography exhibition of old Opry singers. The photos were in black and white, and they captured the faces of the singers in a way that a modern phone cannot. One photo captured a young woman laughing on stage with her guitar. A sign said that flash photography was not allowed, so we only looked.

In the afternoon, we visited the Ryman Auditorium. It was built in 1892 as a church, and from 1943 to 1974 it was the home of the Grand Ole Opry. I really liked the architecture: red brick walls, tall church windows and long benches instead of seats. Our guide said the architecture of the old church gave the room a wonderful sound. There was a little dust on some of the benches, but Dad said the dust only made the place feel more real.

In the evening, we went to see the Grand Ole Opry, which now has its own large building outside the city center. Before we left the hotel, Dad polished his old brown boots until they shone, and he put on his best jacket. "My grandfather always polished his boots before he went out," he said.

The show was the highlight of the weekend. For Dad, the highlight was a song that his grandfather used to love. For me, the highlight was seeing how happy he was. I think I'm a country fan now too.

Questions:
Why does Dad love country music?
He grew up on a farm, and his grandfather used to listen to the Grand Ole Opry on the radio.
What was the special exhibition at the museum about?
It was about the stage clothes of country singers.
What was unusual about the white jacket?
It had small black and white cows on the arms.
What did the old photos capture?
They captured the faces of the old Opry singers.
What did the writer like about the architecture of the Ryman?
The writer liked the red brick walls, the tall church windows and the long benches.
What was the highlight of the weekend?
The show at the Grand Ole Opry was the highlight of the weekend.

lessons.title: A Hot Weekend at the Lake Festival
lessons.summary: A short news report on a three-day summer music festival on the shore of a lake: the heat, the water, the safety plan and the clean-up.
lessons.text:
CLEAR LAKE - The 3-day Clear Lake Music Festival ended on Sunday night after a hot but successful weekend. About 12,000 people came to the festival, which takes place every July on the north shore of the lake. Three stages stood along the shore, and the music went on from the middle of the day until late at night.

On Friday morning, the weather service sent out a heat alert for the whole area. The alert warned that the temperature could reach 98 degrees in the afternoon. The festival sent the alert to every visitor's phone and asked people to drink plenty of liquid, to wear hats and to rest in the shade. "Water is the best liquid on a day like this," said Carla Diaz, who runs the festival. "We told people to drink before they felt they needed it."

The festival had prepared for the heat. The week before, volunteers had used the cold rooms of local restaurants to freeze 20,000 bottles of water. "We freeze the bottles every year," said Ms. Diaz. "If you freeze a bottle, it stays cold for hours, even in the sun." The bottles were free for everyone.

Near the main gate stood the festival headquarters, a large white tent. At the headquarters, visitors could find lost bags, ask for directions or charge their phones. Next to it was a medical tent with 15 qualified nurses and 2 doctors. The qualified staff helped about 60 people, most of whom simply needed water and a cool place to rest.

Local law enforcement officers walked around the festival all weekend. "It was a calm crowd," said one officer. "Law enforcement had a quiet weekend, and that's the best kind."

Families with young children enjoyed the mini stage, where local school bands gave mini concerts of 20 minutes each. Children could also try different instruments next to the mini stage.

This year, the festival used a new ticket system. Last year, someone hacked the festival's ticket website, and some people could not get in with their tickets. "After we were hacked, we chose a safer system," Ms. Diaz explained. "This year, everything worked."

On Monday morning, 200 volunteers cleaned the shore. They collected about 3 tons of trash, and much of the trash will be used again. Ms. Diaz thanked everyone who had helped. "Next year we will have more trash bins and even more water," she said.

Questions:
Where does the festival take place?
It takes place every July on the north shore of Clear Lake.
What did the heat alert warn?
It warned that the temperature could reach 98 degrees in the afternoon.
Why did volunteers freeze 20,000 bottles of water?
They froze the bottles because, if you freeze a bottle, it stays cold for hours, even in the sun.
What could visitors do at the festival headquarters?
They could find lost bags, ask for directions or charge their phones.
Why did the festival use a new ticket system?
Last year, someone hacked the ticket website, so the festival chose a safer system.
How much trash did the volunteers collect?
They collected about 3 tons of trash.

lessons.title: What Your Ears Hear
lessons.summary: A music teacher's newspaper column explains in simple terms how strings make notes, why some notes sound good together, and how to protect your hearing.
lessons.text:
Every year, my new guitar students ask me the same question: what is a note, really? It is a good question, and the answer is simpler than most people think.

When you pick a guitar string, it moves back and forth very quickly. This rapid movement pushes the air around it, and the moving air reaches your ears as sound. The number of times the string moves back and forth in one second is called its frequency. A high frequency gives a high note, whereas a low frequency gives a low note.

Let me give a concrete example. The note that most players use to tune their instruments is an A with a frequency of 440. In other words, the string moves back and forth 440 times every second. That is a rapid movement, far too rapid for the eye to follow.

Now play the next A up the scale, eight notes higher. Its frequency is 880. The two frequencies are 440 and 880 respectively, so the ratio between them is 2 to 1. Notes with a simple ratio sound good together. Another simple ratio is 3 to 2. If you play an A and the E above it, with frequencies of 440 and about 660 respectively, they sound beautiful together, which is why so many songs use them. Notes with a complicated ratio, on the other hand, can sound strange.

Our ears are amazingly sensitive. A young person can hear frequencies from about 20 to about 20,000 times per second. Older people lose some of the highest frequencies, which is completely normal. An old telephone is another concrete example of how frequency matters. Telephone lines used to carry only frequencies between about 300 and 3,400. That is why voices on an old telephone sounded thin.

There is one more thing I always tell my students. Deep inside the ear, there is very sensitive tissue with thousands of tiny hairs. Very loud music can damage this tissue, and once this tissue is damaged, it does not grow back. As long as you keep the volume at a reasonable level and protect your ears at loud concerts, your ears will serve you well for the rest of your life.

Questions:
What is the frequency of a string?
It is the number of times the string moves back and forth in one second.
What concrete example does the writer give first?
The writer gives the example of the A with a frequency of 440, which players use to tune their instruments.
What is the ratio between 440 and 880?
The ratio between them is 2 to 1.
What frequencies can a young person hear?
A young person can hear frequencies from about 20 to about 20,000 times per second.
Why did voices on an old telephone sound thin?
They sounded thin because telephone lines carried only frequencies between about 300 and 3,400.
How can people protect the sensitive tissue in their ears?
They can keep the volume at a reasonable level and protect their ears at loud concerts.

lessons.title: Save the Old Music Hall
lessons.summary: In a calm letter to the local newspaper, a music teacher argues that the city should repair its old concert hall instead of closing it.
lessons.text:
To the Editor:

I am writing about the city council's plan to close the Riverton Music Hall on Main Street. I teach music at Riverton High School, and I am a member of the Riverton Music Alliance, a group of 40 local players, teachers and music store owners. The alliance believes that the council should repair the hall rather than close it.

I understand the council's concerns. The hall was built in 1910, and its roof is in poor condition. Engineers have said that the roof could collapse within a few years if nobody repairs it. Nobody wants a roof to collapse during a concert, so the council plans to withdraw its money from the hall at the end of the year. Nevertheless, I do not believe that the council can justify closing the hall forever. A small saving today cannot justify such a big loss.

First, the hall still yields real benefits for the town. Last year, its concerts yielded about $300,000 in ticket sales, and visitors spent even more in the restaurants and shops on Main Street. If the hall closes, these businesses will lose customers.

Second, the hall may qualify for help from the state. The state has a program for historic buildings, and a building that is more than 100 years old can qualify for it. The program pays half of the cost of repairs. However, the program has one important provision: the building must stay open to the public. Because of this provision, the city would get help only as long as the hall stays open.

Third, the alliance is ready to help the city save money. At the moment, the city pays two full-time workers to do the hall's administrative work, such as booking concerts and answering calls. Our members have offered to do much of this administrative work for free. This would lead to a reduction in costs of about $50,000 a year, and such a reduction would make the repairs much easier to pay for.

I ask the council to weigh the costs and the benefits carefully before it decides. If we weigh them honestly, I believe we will see that it is cheaper to keep the hall than to lose it. The council will discuss the plan on Thursday, and I hope many readers will come.

Linda Moore
Riverton

Questions:
What is the Riverton Music Alliance?
It is a group of 40 local players, teachers and music store owners.
Why does the council plan to withdraw its money from the hall?
Engineers have said that the roof could collapse within a few years.
What benefits does the hall yield for the town?
Its concerts yielded about $300,000 in ticket sales, and visitors spent money in the restaurants and shops.
Why could the hall qualify for help from the state?
It could qualify because it is more than 100 years old.
What is the important provision of the state program?
The building must stay open to the public.
How can the alliance help the city save money?
Its members can do much of the administrative work for free, which would lead to a reduction in costs.

lessons.title: Rock and Roll, Told Simply
lessons.summary: A plain short history of how rock and roll began in the 1950s, why some adults were worried about it, and how it changed popular music.
lessons.text:
Around 1950, young Americans began to listen to a new kind of music. It was fast and loud, and it had a strong beat that made people want to dance. A radio host in Cleveland named Alan Freed played it on his show and helped to make the name "rock and roll" popular.

Rock and roll grew out of rhythm and blues, which was mostly played by Black artists, and it also took ideas from country music and church music. Singers such as Little Richard and Elvis Presley mixed these styles in their own way. You may sometimes hear that one person started rock and roll. That is fiction. In fact, the music grew slowly from the work of many players in many cities.

For many adults, the new music seemed radical. It was much louder than the music that they had grown up with, and the singers moved in ways that they found shocking. There was also something radical about the audience: in a country where Black and white Americans were often kept apart, Black and white teens were buying the same records and dancing to the same songs.

Some adults accused rock and roll of being a bad influence on young people. Some newspapers even accused it of making teens violent. However, most fans were not violent at all. They simply wanted to dance. Many teens went to "sock hops," which were dances held in the school gym. The students took off their shoes so that they would not damage the floor of the gym.

Not everyone who made rock and roll got rich. Many early artists, especially Black artists, were paid very little for their songs, while record companies earned a lot of money. Years later, some of them decided to sue the companies to get the money they were owed. It is not easy to sue a large company, and not all of them won.

By 1960, rock and roll had begun to dominate American radio. Rock music continued to grow, and for several decades it continued to dominate popular music in America and around the world. Today, other kinds of music are more popular, but almost every modern style owes something to rock and roll.

Questions:
Who helped to make the name "rock and roll" popular?
A radio host in Cleveland named Alan Freed helped to make it popular.
What kinds of music did rock and roll grow out of?
It grew out of rhythm and blues, and it also took ideas from country music and church music.
Why is it fiction that one person started rock and roll?
It is fiction because the music grew slowly from the work of many players.
What was rock and roll accused of?
Some adults accused it of being a bad influence on young people.
Why did students take off their shoes at sock hops?
They took off their shoes so that they would not damage the floor of the gym.
Why did some players decide to sue record companies?
They decided to sue them to get the money they were owed.

lessons.title: My Cousin from London Visits Memphis
lessons.summary: A young man shows his British cousin around Memphis in the fall: Beale Street, Sun Studio, Graceland and a lot of barbecue.
lessons.text:
Last October, my cousin Olivia came from London to visit us in Memphis for a week. It was her first trip to America. She said she had always wanted to see America in the autumn. Here in Tennessee we usually call it fall, but Olivia calls it autumn, and by the end of the week I was saying autumn too.

Olivia speaks English, of course, but some of her words are different from ours. She calls her mother "Mum," whereas I call mine "Mom." On the first evening, she telephoned her mum in London to say that she had arrived.

Before the trip, Olivia had changed some British pounds into dollars at a bank. She found our currency difficult at first. "All your paper money is the same size, and most of it is green," she said. "In Britain, every bill is a different size and color. And we call them notes, not bills." By the third day, she was used to the new currency.

On our first day, we walked along Beale Street, where blues singers have played for more than 100 years. In the evening, we listened to a blues band in a small club. The next morning, we visited Sun Studio, the small building where Elvis Presley made his first records. Olivia stood in the same room where he had once stood, and she said she could hardly believe it.

On the third day, we drove to Graceland, Elvis Presley's home. We walked through the house and then went out to the garden behind it. That is where his grave is. His grave lies next to the graves of his parents and his grandmother. Olivia said it was a quiet and beautiful place.

Of course, nobody can visit Memphis without eating barbecue. We ate at a famous restaurant in the city center, and Olivia ate until her stomach hurt. "My stomach is full for the rest of the week," she said. However, late that night we were both hungry again, so we raided the kitchen. We took out everything we could find: cold meat, bread, cheese and half a cake. In the morning, my mom laughed when she saw the empty plates. "Who raided my kitchen?" she asked.

At the airport, Olivia said it had been the best week of her life. She promised to come back next autumn, and I promised to visit her and her mum in London.

Questions:
Why does Olivia say "autumn"?
She is from London, and in Britain people call that season autumn.
What does Olivia call her mother?
She calls her mother "Mum."
Why did Olivia find the American currency difficult?
All the paper money is the same size, and most of it is green.
What did Olivia and her cousin visit on the second morning?
They visited Sun Studio, where Elvis Presley made his first records.
Where is Elvis Presley's grave?
His grave is in the garden behind his home, Graceland, next to the graves of his parents and his grandmother.
What did they do late that night?
They were hungry again, so they raided the kitchen.
